claims.text: The Afsluitdijk is a dam and causeway in the Netherlands, built between 1927 and 1932, running from Den Oever in North Holland to the village of Zurich in Friesland over a length of 32 kilometres.
It dammed off the Zuiderzee, a salt water inlet of the North Sea, and turned it into the fresh water lake of the IJsselmeer.
The dyke was closed on 28 May 1932, and it was officially opened on 25 September 1933.

On 13 and 14 January 1916 the dikes at several places along the Zuiderzee broke in a winter storm and the land behind them flooded; this was the decisive impetus to implement the plans to tame the Zuiderzee.
The initial body of water affected by the project was 3,500 square kilometres.
Ten thousand workers, 27 large dredges, 13 floating cranes, 132 barges and 88 tugs worked on the project at the end.
Two complexes of locks and sluices, at Den Oever and at Kornwerderzand, hold 25 discharge sluices that routinely let water out of the lake, which rivers keep feeding.
The Wieringermeer, a 200 km2 polder, was dammed in 1929 and fully drained in 1930; the Flevolands, almost 1,000 km2, were drained after the war.
A new province, Flevoland, was created out of the Noordoostpolder and the Flevolands in 1986.
Major upgrade works commenced in 2019 and will raise the dam by approximately 2 metres.
